l: steel ingot, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
s: A steel ingot contains apparent and latent heat in excess of that required for rolling. After being stripped, it is placed in a heated soaking pit, where its internal heat is redistributed and its surface becomes hot enough for rolling without a conventional reheating operation.

l: rolling of steel ingots, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
s: Rolling of steel ingots can be performed after the ingots have soaked for approximately 20–30 minutes. The treated ingots can be sent directly to the rolls, and the text reports satisfactory double-head rails produced by this method.

l: heating furnace, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
s: The heating furnace is the previously universal means of reheating steel ingots before rolling. The soaking pit process is presented as a way to dispense with such furnaces, the fuel they consume, their gas generators, their maintenance, and losses caused by oxidation or overheating.

l: blooming mill, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
s: The blooming mill receives ingots removed from the soaking pits and swung to its live rollers by a crane. The machinery at Darlington was not adapted for rolling off in one heat, although it successfully bloomed the treated ingots and directly rolled some double-head rails.

l: ingot crane, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
s: The ingot crane places stripped ingots into the soaking pits and later removes them and swings them to the blooming mill. The recommended arrangement uses a crane capable of commanding both the pits and the mill's live rollers; with such a crane, four men and a boy could pass the full make through the pits.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: L. Clemandot devised a method called tempering by compression for treating metals, especially steel. The process heats metal to a cherry red, compresses it strongly, and maintains pressure until it cools completely. The resulting metal is exceedingly hard, has contracted molecularly, and has a fine grain that resembles polished nickel. Compressed steel also acquires coercitive force and retains magnetism, with no loss observed after three months.

l: L. Clemandot, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: L. Clemandot devised a method of treating metals, especially steel, called tempering by compression.

l: tempering by compression, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: Tempering by compression consists of heating metal to a cherry red, compressing it strongly, and maintaining the pressure until the metal is completely cooled. The process produces effects resembling tempering, including great hardness, molecular contraction, and fine grain.

l: metals, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: Metals can be treated by heating them to a cherry red and compressing them until they cool. Compression modifies their molecular state, and hydraulic pressure has a greater effect than hammering or hardening.

l: fluid steel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: Steel treated by compression becomes exceedingly hard and develops molecular contraction and a fine grain. Compressed steel also acquires coercitive force and retains its magnetism, with no loss observed after three months.

l: compression, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: Compression is applied strongly to heated metal and maintained until the metal is completely cooled. Its effect is described as greater than that of hammering and hardening, especially when those operations are performed on nearly cold metal.

l: pressure, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: Pressure is maintained during cooling in tempering by compression. The operation can be measured and graduated, allowing tempering at a specified pressure, and hydraulic pressure is said to have a particularly strong effect.

l: tempering, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: Tempering and tempering by compression produce similar results. Their phenomena may involve molecular approximation and amorphism, producing homogeneity through the absence of crystallization.

l: coercitive force, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: Compressed steel acquires coercitive force, which enables it to absorb magnetism. Its relationship to the durability of compressed steel is identified as requiring study.

l: magnetism, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
s: Compressed steel acquires magnetism-absorbing properties through coercitive force. Experiments had shown no loss of magnetism after three months.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: In “Economical Steam Power,” William Barnet Le Van explains that economical steam power depends on the coordinated arrangement of engines, boilers, and transmission accessories. He compares single and subdivided power systems, engine forms, condensing and non-condensing engines, and different engine classes according to their first cost, operating hours, fuel, water, repairs, and depreciation. Using a flouring mill in Philadelphia as an example, he shows that replacing two engines with one first-class automatic engine greatly reduced coal and feed-water consumption and saved $4,954 over 300 operating days.

l: Economical Steam Power, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: Economical steam power requires a judicious arrangement of engines, boilers, and transmission accessories. William Barnet Le Van emphasizes that the most economical choice depends on the plant's circumstances, operating schedule, fuel and water costs, and required power.

l: William Barnet Le Van, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: William Barnet Le Van argues that steam-power users often fail to consider how the costs and operating conditions of engines, boilers, and accessories affect economy. He illustrates his argument with calculations comparing two engines with one first-class automatic engine.

l: steam power, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: Steam power can be made more economical through careful plant planning and by selecting equipment suited to the particular situation. Dividing power among several engines can reduce shafting and transmission costs and limit the effects of stoppages.

l: engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: An engine should be selected by considering its first cost, fuel consumption, operating hours, lubrication, repairs, depreciation, and boiler requirements. Le Van states that engines driving manufactories generally cannot be too high a class because fuel savings usually outweigh the interest on their additional first cost.

l: boiler, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: Boilers are one of the principal components whose first cost and interest charges must be considered. A non-condensing engine operated at high steam pressure may require a stronger boiler, potentially offsetting the additional cost of a condensing engine.

l: horizontal engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: The horizontal engine is described as the best form in most cases where machinery must be driven, particularly for large powers. It is said to be more durable and less expensive than a beam engine, capable of higher speed, and less demanding in engine-house and foundation costs.

l: condensing engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: A well-constructed condensing engine is generally economically preferable when sufficient condensing water is available at moderate cost. Its greater economy is said to justify the additional purchase cost except in very small-power cases or where exhaust steam from a non-condensing engine can be used for heating or drying.

l: automatic engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: An automatic engine costs more than a plain slide-valve engine but can reduce fuel, lubrication, repair, depreciation, and boiler-power costs. In the cited flouring mill example, one first-class automatic engine replaced two engines and reduced the stated annual coal and water costs from $11,503 to $6,560.

l: mill, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: A mill's economical power arrangement depends on its required total power and the relationship among its engines, boilers, transmission equipment, and operating conditions. Dividing power among several engines can allow one department to stop while the others continue operating.

l: flouring mill in Philadelphia, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: The flouring mill in Philadelphia operated two engines rated at seventy indicated horsepower each for an average of twenty-four hours per day on 300 days per year. After replacement by one automatic engine developing 142 horsepower, the stated coal and water costs fell from $11,503 to $6,560, producing a reported annual saving of $4,954.

l: Philadelphia, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: Philadelphia is identified as the location of the flouring mill example and as a city where water was charged at three dollars per horsepower per annum. First-class engines were charged the same water rate as inferior engines despite their lower water consumption.

l: coal, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: Coal is a major operating cost in steam power, and its price and the engine's hourly consumption determine whether a more expensive engine is economical. In the example, coal consumption fell from five and one-half pounds to three pounds per hour per horsepower, reducing the stated 300-day cost from $11,088 to $6,134.

l: feed water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: Feed water consumption is used as a measure of engine economy. The two original engines required 40,320,000 pounds annually, while the replacement engine required 30,672,000 pounds, a reported saving of 9,648,000 pounds, or 31.4 percent.

l: replacement of the two engines, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
s: The replacement of the two engines with one first-class automatic engine produced the same stated work with lower coal and feed-water consumption. The reported total cost of coal and water decreased by $4,954 over 300 days.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: River improvements near St. Louis on the Mississippi River are progressing satisfactorily through jetty construction, mattress placement, bank revetment, and related work. At Twin Hollow, Carroll's Island, and Beard's Island, engineers are addressing sand bars and protecting or concentrating the river channel. About 1,200 men, thirty barges and scows, two steam launches, and the stern-wheel steamer A. A. Humphreys are employed. The work has cost about $200,000, and an appropriation of approximately $600,000 for the ensuing year offers prospects for a clear channel.

l: river improvements near St. Louis, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: The improvements are progressing satisfactorily. They employ jetty construction, mattresses, hurdles, willow interweaving, and stone revetments to improve the river channel.

l: Mississippi River, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: The Mississippi River near St. Louis is being improved to concentrate its stream, prevent widening, and provide a clear channel.

l: St. Louis, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: St. Louis is the location near which the Mississippi River improvements are being carried out. Twin Hollow lies thirteen miles from St. Louis.

l: jetty system, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: The jetty system is described as effective, with lines of mattresses accumulating sand deposits from the river surface to nearly sixteen feet high.

l: mattresses, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: Mattresses have accumulated sand deposits near the surface of the river to nearly sixteen feet in height. At Carroll's Island, mattresses 125 feet wide have been placed, and 4,000 feet have been begun at Beard's Island.

l: Twin Hollow, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: Twin Hollow is thirteen miles from St. Louis and six miles from Horse-Tail Bar. Engineering forces are working there on a sand bar extending across the widest portion of the river.

l: sand bar (at Twin Hollow), Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: The sand bar at Twin Hollow extends over the widest portion of the river. Hurdles are built from the shore to concentrate the stream on the obstruction, while willows interwoven between piles protect the river from widening.

l: Carroll's Island, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: At Carroll's Island, 125-foot-wide mattresses have been placed and the banks have been revetted with stone from ordinary low water to a 16-foot stage. There is plenty of water over the bar, with a minimum reported depth of twelve feet.

l: Beard's Island, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: Beard's Island is also being improved and has the largest force of men engaged at any one place. Four thousand feet of mattresses have been begun there, with work expected to continue until floating ice suspends operations.

l: men employed on the improvements, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: About 1,200 men are employed on the improvements. They are working across the different river sections, including Beard's Island.

l: W. F. Fries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: W. F. Fries is the resident engineer directing the different sections of the improvements.

l: E. M. Currie, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: E. M. Currie is the superintending engineer directing the different sections of the improvements.

l: appropriation for the ensuing year, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: The appropriation for the ensuing year approximates $600,000. It follows about $200,000 in actual money already expended on the improvements.

l: clear channel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
s: The prospect of a clear channel is described as gratifying to those interested in the river, in light of the ongoing improvements and the appropriation for the ensuing year.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Dr. Buente's burette is presented as a simpler and more easily operated apparatus for analyzing blast-furnace gases than the various Orsat apparatus. The procedure describes filling the burette, measuring gas volumes, and absorbing carbonic acid, oxygen, and oxide of carbon with specified liquids. Combustion in a heated tube, using atmospheric air and a palladium wire, permits quantitative analysis of hydrogen and oxide of carbon. Changes in gas volume after absorption or combustion are used to calculate the proportions of the gases.

l: Bunte's burette, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Bunte's burette is used for the analysis of furnace gases and is described as simpler to use than the apparatus of Orsat. It permits rapid absorption of oxide of carbon and measures gas composition from volume contractions after absorption or combustion.

l: Dr. Buente, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Dr. Buente devised the burette used for analyzing blast-furnace gases.

l: blast-furnace gases, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Blast-furnace gases are analyzed with the burette by measuring their initial volume and determining the contractions caused by absorption and combustion.

l: gas analysis, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Gas analysis with the apparatus involves filling the burette, restoring the gas to its original pressure, and measuring volume changes after chemical absorption or combustion.

l: absorbing liquid, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: The absorbing liquid for oxide of carbon is prepared from saturated copper chloride in hydrochloric acid with a small quantity of dissolved tin chloride and spirals of red copper. Caustic potassa or pyrogallate of potassa is used for other absorptions, and the liquids can be replaced or washed out before measurement.

l: caustic potassa, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Caustic potassa is sucked into the burette to absorb carbonic acid. It is also used with pyrogallic acid and potash to determine oxygen, and it is allowed to enter after combustion when analyzing oxide of carbon.

l: pyrogallate of potassa, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Pyrogallate of potassa is used to absorb oxygen after carbonic acid has been removed with caustic potassa. It must be completely removed from the burette before the acid copper chloride solution is introduced.

l: oxide of carbon, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: The burette permits rapid absorption of oxide of carbon, although part of the absorbing liquid must be replaced three or four times for the last fractions. Oxide of carbon can also be quantitatively analyzed by combustion, with the total contraction from combustion and absorption multiplied by two-thirds giving its volume.

l: carbonic acid, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Carbonic acid is absorbed by caustic potassa, and the resulting diminution in gas volume gives its volume in a combustion smoke analysis. Combustion of oxide of carbon produces an equal volume of carbonic acid.

l: oxygen, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Oxygen is determined after carbonic acid has been absorbed by allowing an aqueous solution of pyrogallic acid and potash to enter the burette. Its presence darkens the liquid, and agitation continues until no further absorption occurs.

l: hydrogen, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Hydrogen is analyzed by combustion with atmospheric air in the heated combustion tube. The contraction caused by burning it, multiplied by two-thirds, gives the original volume of hydrogen burned.

l: water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Water fills the burette and funnel, drives gas into or out of the apparatus, and establishes the pressure needed for measurement. It is also used to wash absorbing liquids from the burette, except that dilute hydrochloric acid is used when an acid copper chloride solution is employed.

l: combustion tube, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: The combustion tube is heated to redness by a Bunsen burner or alcohol lamp. A mixture of gas and atmospheric air passes through it in the presence of a palladium wire, causing combustion.

l: combustion of gas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
s: Combustion of gas is carried out by mixing the burette gas with atmospheric air and passing the mixture through the heated combustion tube. After cooling and restoring the original pressure, the contraction is measured to calculate hydrogen or oxide of carbon.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE "UNIVERSAL" GAS ENGINE.
s: The Universal gas engine was invented by J. A. Ewins and H. Newman and made by T. B. Barker of Birmingham. It is a simple, single-acting gas engine made in sizes from one-eighth to one horse-power, with larger sizes being developed. Its main new feature is a rotary ignition valve that uses radial slots to pass flame into the cylinder and ignite the gas-air charge. The engines were reported to work successfully and to have low operating costs.

l: Universal gas engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE "UNIVERSAL" GAS ENGINE.
s: The Universal gas engine is a simple, single-acting engine invented by J. A. Ewins and H. Newman and made by T. B. Barker. It was constructed in sizes from one-eighth horse-power to one horse-power, with larger sizes being made, and was reported to work successfully at low gas cost.

l: gas engine design, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE "UNIVERSAL" GAS ENGINE.
s: The design draws an explosive mixture of gas and air into the cylinder and ignites it once per revolution without compressing the charge. It uses valve and ignition mechanisms that can be duplicated at the front end to make the engine double-acting, while an eccentric keeps the exhaust valve open during the return stroke.

l: rotary ignition, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE "UNIVERSAL" GAS ENGINE.
s: The rotary ignition consists of a ratchet plate or flat disk with small radial slots that successively align with a slot at the end of the cylinder. When aligned, flame from the igniting gas jet passes through the openings and ignites the charge; the mechanism has a very small range of motion and is described as requiring no lubrication or attention.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
s: The gas furnace for baking refractory products is a smaller annular furnace designed for small establishments, with a baking chamber set into the ground and covered by movable refractory-clay slabs. Gas enters through channels, pipes, and vertical conduits before emerging through tuyeres into the baking chamber. A smoking furnace supplies hot gases for preliminary heating, with adjustable cold-air intake allowing its output temperature to vary from about 30 to 50 degrees upward. The smoking apparatus heated by gas avoids the cinders, dust, and difficult gradual heating associated with ordinary smoking systems.

l: gas furnace for baking refractory products, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
s: The gas furnace for baking refractory products has a baking chamber only one and a half meters high and covered by removable refractory-clay slabs rather than a vault. A small car on a movable track removes each slab from an emptied compartment and places it over a newly filled compartment. Gas passes through channel G, pipe a, vertical conduits b, and tuyeres into the chamber.

l: refractory products, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
s: Refractory products are baked in the furnace's chamber. The chamber is gradually heated, and the products are not exposed to cinders or dust from the heating process.

l: smoking furnace, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
s: The smoking furnace, S, provides gas-heated preliminary heating or smoking. Air enters through apertures in its cover, combustion produces very hot gases, and these gases pass through tube e and vertical conduits b' into the smoking chamber. Adjustable registers admit cold, dry air to vary the temperature of the gases released through tube e.

l: smoking apparatus heated by gas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
s: The smoking apparatus heated by gas eliminates the cinders and dust associated with the ordinary system and makes gradual heating of objects to be baked easier. At the beginning, cold air lowers the smoke-gas temperature to 30 or 50 degrees; the air entrances are then gradually closed to increase the temperature as desired.

l: gas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
s: Gas enters the furnace through channel G, pipe a, and vertical conduits before being discharged through tuyeres into the baking chamber. In the smoking furnace, gas passes through tube t, where it is mixed with air and burned, producing hot gases that are directed into the smoking chamber.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE EFFICIENCY OF FANS.
s: The unit explains the work required to move air and the factors affecting the efficiency of fans. It describes how blade shape, speed, area, and casing influence air motion, power consumption, noise, and pressure. It presents a calculation estimating the power and air delivery of a fan, while noting that such efficiency is not achieved in practice. Mr. Buckle's recommended fan proportions for pressures of 3 to 6 ounces per square inch are also given.

l: efficiency of fans, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE EFFICIENCY OF FANS.
s: The efficiency of fans depends more on their proportions than on blade shapes, provided that easy curves and no sharp angles are used. Blade and case designs influence noise and modify efficiency, especially at high speeds, but recorded experiments are few and much ignorance remains about true efficiency.

l: fan, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE EFFICIENCY OF FANS.
s: A fan puts the weight of air in motion, overcoming inertia and frictional resistances. Air enters at the center and escapes at the circumference, with its motion changed through a right angle; gradually curved blades reduce violent deflection and noise. The fan's power requirement depends on blade area, air pressure, and the velocity of the center of effort, while its casing should widen as an arithmetical spiral toward the discharge opening.

l: atmospheric air, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE EFFICIENCY OF FANS.
s: Air possesses weight, with approximately 13.141 cubic feet weighing one pound at a pressure of 14.7 pounds per square inch and a temperature of 62 degrees. In a fan, air is accelerated outward by centrifugal force and tends to move tangentially to the blade path rather than directly radially. The pressure against the blades corresponds to the weight of a column of air whose height is determined by the air's velocity.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
s: The unit concerns the utilization of coal refuse to manufacture agglomerated artificial fuel for railways, steamboats, industry, and domestic heating. It describes the preparation of coal refuse, including sifting, washing, partial drying, mixing with coal dust and pitch, crushing, steaming, and conversion into a plastic paste. It also describes Bilan's machine, which compresses the paste into spherical conglomerates using four coordinated moulding wheels. The machine can produce about 40 tons of globular artificial fuel per day.

l: coal refuse, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
s: Coal refuse is sifted to separate dust from coal grains, with the nut size removed and sold separately. The grains are washed by size, partially drained or dried, then mixed with coal dust and eight to ten percent broken coal pitch before being crushed and formed into fuel.

l: artificial fuel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
s: Artificial fuel made from coal refuse is an agglomerated fuel used on railways and steamboats, in industry, and for domestic heating. Bilan's machine produces it in spherical or globular form.

l: agglomerating machine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
s: An agglomerating machine should be simple, accessible for cleaning, and designed to permit worn parts to be changed with minimal interruption. It should apply powerful, progressive compression over as much of the conglomerate's surface as possible and remove the product from the mould without relying on fouling pistons or springs.

l: manufacture of artificial fuel from coal refuse, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
s: The manufacture involves sifting and classifying the refuse, washing and partly drying the coal grains, mixing them with coal dust and pitch, crushing the mixture, converting it into a plastic paste with superheated steam, and distributing it into moulds for compression.

l: plastic paste, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
s: The coal mixture becomes a plastic paste in a pug-mill when superheated steam is admitted. The paste is then led into an agitator to remove steam and distribute the material into the moulds of the compressing machine.

l: spherical conglomerates, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
s: Spherical conglomerates are formed when four vertical moulding wheels, each carrying quarter-sphere cavities, meet and enclose the paste. After further rotation separates the wheels, the finished balls drop out.

l: Bilan, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
s: Bilan is associated with the machine shown for manufacturing spherical conglomerates intended for domestic purposes.

l: Bilan's machine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
s: Bilan's machine has a cast-iron frame supporting four vertical moulding wheels arranged at right angles, along with a hopper, vertical helices, shafts, screws, gears, and beveled pinions. The wheels progressively compress the paste from four quarters, and their mould-carrying segments can be removed and replaced when worn. The machine produces about 40 tons of globular artificial fuel per day.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
s: The unit describes a hank sizing and wringing machine made by Heywood & Spencer of Radcliffe, near Manchester. The machine uses geared hooks to twist hanks, hold them briefly while excess size is wiped off, and then reverse the twist before removal. It can be used for sizing and fancy dyeing, with running performed on one side while finishing is performed on the other. The makers claim production rates of about 36 10-pound bundles per hour at finishing and 45 bundles in 2-pound wringers at running.

l: Hank sizing and wringing machine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
s: The hank sizing and wringing machine consists of two vats with driving gear between them and hooks whose spacing can be adjusted to the length or size of the hanks. It twists hanks, holds them briefly for excess size to be wiped off, reverses the twist, and removes them by hand or with a lifting lattice.

l: Heywood & Spencer, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
s: Heywood & Spencer, of Radcliffe, near Manchester, made the hank sizing machine described. The makers claim that a double machine can finish about 36 10-pound bundles per hour or run about 45 bundles in 2-pound wringers.

l: hank, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
s: The hank is lifted from a vat and placed on the machine's hooks. It is twisted two, two and a half, three, or more times, held while excess size is wiped off, then untwisted and removed for transport to the drying stove.

l: sizing, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
s: Sizing uses a customary double operation consisting of running followed by finishing. The machine can perform running on one side while finishing occurs on the other, and it can also run on both sides if required.

l: wringing, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
s: Wringing hanks by hand is described as severe labor that limits production and can make even colors difficult to obtain in dyeing. The machine is intended to carry out this heavy work more quickly and reliably.

l: running, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
s: Running is the first operation in sizing and can be carried on one side while finishing occurs on the other, or on both sides. The makers claim a production rate of about 45 bundles in 2-pound wringers.

l: finishing, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
s: Finishing is the second operation in sizing and can be performed simultaneously with running on the opposite side. The makers claim a production rate of about 36 10-pound bundles per hour at finishing.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVED COKE BREAKER.
s: The improved coke breaker used by the South Metropolitan Gas Company consists of a single drum with cutting edges that breaks coke against a fixed grid. Its capacity can be changed by adding or removing cast rings, while the grid distance controls the fineness of the broken coke. The machine requires little power, produces relatively little waste, and can separate the output into larger coke, clean breeze, and dust. At full capacity, it can break about 8 tons per hour, and broken coke generally sells for 2s. to 2s. 6d. more per ton than large coke.

l: improved coke breaker, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVED COKE BREAKER.
s: The improved coke breaker uses a single revolving drum with cutting edges to break coke against a fixed grid, without toothed gearing. Its capacity is adjusted by varying the number of cast rings, and the fineness of the product is controlled by changing the grid's distance from the drum. It can be made in different sizes, including hand-powered versions, and the full-size machine can break about 8 tons of coke per hour.

l: South Metropolitan Gas Company, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVED COKE BREAKER.
s: The South Metropolitan Gas Company uses the improved coke breaker. A full-size machine at its Old Kent Road works was driven by a one horse power Otto gas-engine and broke two tons of coke in half an hour during a trial.

l: coke, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVED COKE BREAKER.
s: Coke is broken by the improved coke breaker and screened into larger coke, clean breeze, and dust. The dust is used at the works to mix with lime in the purifiers. Broken coke generally fetches 2s. to 2s. 6d. more per ton than large coke, while the machine produces only a small quantity of waste.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVEMENT IN PRINTING MACHINERY.
s: The improvement in printing machinery is the design of Alfred Godfrey of Clapton. It uses a vibrating rack, A, and a pinion, a1, supported by a radial arm, a2, mounted on the shaft, a3, which supports the driving wheel, a4. The arrangement is intended to transmit easy, uniform, and silent motion to the rack and table through the vibrating movement of the arm, pinion, and rack.

l: improvement in printing machinery, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVEMENT IN PRINTING MACHINERY.
s: It employs a vibrating rack, A, and a pinion, a1, supported by a radial arm, a2, mounted on the shaft, a3. The arrangement transmits an easy, uniform, and silent motion to the rack and table.

l: Alfred Godfrey, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVEMENT IN PRINTING MACHINERY.
s: Alfred Godfrey, of Clapton, designed the improvement in printing machinery.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: The unit describes a mining rush in Southern New Mexico, centered on the newly active Perche district near Lake Valley and Hillsboro. Jack Shedd made the first great strike in the Perche district on August 15, finding surface blocks of exceptionally rich silver ore. The discovery drew about 2,000 prospectors and led to more than 1,000 claims, while properties such as the Solitaire and Bullion attracted investors and development. The Perche district appeared likely to become a major mining center despite uncertainty about some discoveries.

l: mining rush, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: The mining rush spread through the Perche district after reports of rich silver discoveries, drawing about 2,000 people and producing more than 1,000 located prospects. The excitement was compared with the speculative enthusiasm of mining-stock buyers in New York.

l: Southern New Mexico, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: Southern New Mexico is presented as a prospective mining center because of the activity around Lake Valley, the Black Range, and especially the Perche district.

l: Lake Valley, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: Lake Valley had previously been considered likely to become the central mining camp of the region. News of discoveries in the Perche district caused workers and prospectors to leave Lake Valley and head there.

l: Perche district, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: The Perche district lies on the eastern flanks of the Mimbres Mountains, about twenty-five miles northwest of Lake Valley and ten miles west of Hillsboro. Rich discoveries, including the Solitaire and Bullion, brought intense excitement and made the district's future appear assured.

l: prospectors, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: Prospectors rapidly entered the Perche district after the first discoveries, arriving on foot, on mules, and with minimal supplies. Within a month, roughly 2,000 prospectors and other people were there, and more than 1,000 prospects had been located.

l: Mimbres Mountains, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: The Mimbres Mountains are part of the Rocky Mountain range and run generally north and south, parallel to the Rio Grande and about forty miles west of it. The Perche district is located on their eastern flanks.

l: Black Range, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: The northern half of the Mimbres Mountains is known as the Black Range. It experienced mining excitement about a year and a half earlier, and the reopening of the Ivanhoe was expected to stimulate the region.

l: Hillsboro, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: Hillsboro is a promising mining town about ten miles east of the Perche district, with some mills and approximately 300 people. Three forks of the Perche River unite there.

l: Jack Shedd, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: Jack Shedd, who had discovered the Robinson mine in Colorado, was prospecting near the south branch of the north fork of the Perche River on August 15 when he made the district's first great strike. He found surface pieces and large blocks of exceptionally rich silver ore, and his location, the Solitaire, later attracted the interest of ex-Governor Tabor and Mr. Wurtzbach.

l: first great strike in the Perche district, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: The first great strike in the Perche district consisted of surface float found on a heavily timbered ridge by Jack Shedd. It included a 150-pound lump of ore worth an average of $11 per pound and an 87-pound block of horn silver containing specimens nearly 75 percent silver.

l: Solitaire, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: The Solitaire was Jack Shedd's location and showed what appeared to be a contact vein with porphyry and limestone walls, in places forming a thirty-foot-wide ledge. Its quartz vein carried sulphides and visible horn silver, with reported average assays of $350 to $500, but a later claim that it was only a blind lead lacked confirmation.

l: ex-Governor Tabor, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: Ex-Governor Tabor was reported to have bought the Solitaire from Jack Shedd for $100,000 on August 25, but that report was described as untrue. His representative had examined the properties, and the Governor had apparently bonded the mine while viewing it favorably.

l: silver ore, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
s: Silver ore discovered in the Perche district included native silver, silver sulphides, horn silver, and quartz carrying sulphides. The reported discoveries ranged from exceptionally rich surface specimens to ore in the Bullion and other developing properties.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE SOY BEAN.
s: The unit concerns the Soy bean and its nutritional qualities and uses. The British Medical Journal reports that Prof. E. Kinch describes it as more like animal food than any other known vegetable production because it is rich in fat and albuminoids. It is widely used as food in China and Japan, has been cultivated with fair success in Italy and France, and provides foods and useful fodder from its straw.

l: Soy bean, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE SOY BEAN.
s: The Soy bean is described as being singularly rich in fat and albuminoids, and as approaching more nearly to animal food than any other known vegetable production. It is largely used as food in China and Japan; efforts to acclimatize it in Europe have achieved fair success in Italy and France. Many foods are made from it, and its straw is useful fodder.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: W.H. Preece describes a new arc electric lamp and the system invented by M. Abdank. The system separates the regulator from the lamp, allowing the lamp to be installed in inaccessible locations while the regulator remains accessible. A balance using two solenoids controls a break that makes minute adjustments to the carbon electrodes as carbon is consumed, maintaining a steady electric arc. An automatic cut-off protects series-connected lamps by replacing a failed lamp with an equivalent resistance.

l: W.H. Preece, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: W.H. Preece presented the new arc electric lamp to the Section and revised the paper describing it. He reported that the lamp operated with constant steadiness.

l: new arc electric lamp, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: The new arc electric lamp has a fixed negative carbon and a movable positive carbon. Its regulation is separated from the lamp, allowing the lamp to be fixed in an inaccessible place.

l: arc electric lighting, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: Arc electric lighting is affected by the consumption of its carbon electrodes, which can cause flickering and irregularity. The described system aims to make the light steady through automatic, very small adjustments.

l: M. Abdank, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: M. Abdank invented the system described by W.H. Preece. His system separates the regulator from the lamp and uses automatic regulation.

l: Abdank lamp system, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: The Abdank lamp system uses an external regulator consisting of a balance and a cut-off. It regulates the carbon gap in short successive steps and includes an automatic cut-off for accidents when several lamps are connected in series.

l: regulator, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: The regulator is separated from the lamp and may be placed where it can be inspected and manipulated easily. It uses a balance and a cut-off to compensate for carbon consumption and maintain the required electrical resistance.

l: carbon electrodes, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: The bottom or negative carbon is fixed, while the top or positive carbon moves vertically. The positive carbon is lifted when current energizes an electromagnet, and the regulator later allows the carbons to approach by about 0.01 to 0.02 millimeter at a time.

l: electromagnet, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: An electromagnet lifts the rod carrying the positive carbon when current passes through its coil. Another electromagnet controls the break that releases the rack and permits the carbons to approach.

l: lamp balance, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: The lamp balance consists of two solenoids: one carrying the main current and one carrying a shunt current. Changes in current alter their opposing magnetic effects, causing an iron rod to break or restore contact and thereby control the lamp's adjustment.

l: automatic cut-off, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: The automatic cut-off is used when several lamps are connected in series. If a lamp fails or a carbon breaks, it connects the circuit through a resistance equivalent to the lamp, allowing the other lamps to continue operating and enabling rapid relighting when contact is restored.

l: dynamo machine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: The dynamo machine supplies the current to the series-connected lamps. Its positive lead passes through the balance and the lamps before returning to its negative pole.

l: series-connected lamps, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: Series-connected lamps receive current successively from the dynamo machine, with the current returning from each lamp to the balance and then proceeding to the next. The automatic cut-off allows a failed lamp to be bypassed by a resistance.

l: electric arc, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: The electric arc forms when the electromagnet lifts the positive carbon away from the negative carbon. It continues to burn steadily while the current remains constant, with the regulator compensating for increased resistance as the arc changes.

l: carbon consumption, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: Carbon consumption changes the distance and resistance between the electrodes. The regulator compensates by allowing the carbon support to fall in continual, nearly invisible increments.

l: flickering and irregularity of light, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
s: Flickering and irregularity of light are attributed to variations in the consumption of the carbons. The Abdank system is intended to prevent these effects through small and rapid regulatory movements that do not affect the main current.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
s: The unit concerns methods and apparatus for obtaining clean or distilled water for photographic use. It explains that rain-water collected after roofs have been washed can provide clean soft water, and describes an automatic shunt for diverting the initial dirty flow. It also discusses glass and metal distillation apparatus for preparing highly pure water, especially for nitrate baths and emulsions. The text details photographic problems caused by chlorides, lime, calcium oxalate, and other impurities in water.

l: apparatus for obtaining pure water for photographic use, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
s: The apparatus includes an automatic shunt for diverting rain-water until a roof has been washed, as well as glass and metal stills for distillation. The text recommends distilled water for nitrate baths and emulsion preparation.

l: water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
s: Naturally occurring water contains dissolved inorganic and organic impurities and gases. Impurities in water can shorten the effectiveness of iron and pyrogallic developers, produce calcium oxalate veils on negatives, and affect silver prints and carbon printing.

l: rain-water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
s: Rain-water collected in a secluded district after previous rain can be exceptionally pure, containing little more than traces of carbonic acid and other atmospheric gases. In towns, especially when it flows over dirty roofs, it can become contaminated, but clean rain-water collected after the roofs are washed is valuable for photographic work.

l: distilled water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
s: Distilled water is recommended for preparing the nitrate bath and should always be used in preparing emulsion. It can be produced in a glass apparatus or in a metal still with a tin condensing worm, provided the apparatus is kept clean.

l: soft water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
s: Clean soft water is useful for photographic processes because developers remain effective longer and carbon printing can be carried out more rapidly or at a lower temperature. Soft water collected from dirty roofs, however, may contain substantial carbonaceous and organic contamination.

l: automatic shunt for diverting rainwater, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
s: The automatic shunt prevents water from entering a cistern until the roof has been thoroughly washed. Its operation depends on a valve, lever, weight, and vessel with a small hole that restores the apparatus after rain ceases; careful adjustment of these parts is required.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, [Illustration] BLACK PHOSPHORUS.
s: P. Thenard examines black, or dark gray, phosphorus and challenges the view that it is always ordinary phosphorus mixed with traces of a metallic phosphide. A specimen became white when melted and stayed white after sudden cooling, but turned black again when allowed to become superfused and then contacted with white or black phosphorus. When part of the specimen was dissolved in carbon disulphide, only a trace of very pale yellow matter remained undissolved, appearing to be amorphous phosphorus.

l: BLACK PHOSPHORUS, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, [Illustration] BLACK PHOSPHORUS.
s: Black phosphorus is described as possibly not always being a mixture of ordinary phosphorus and traces of a metallic phosphide. A dark gray specimen became white when melted and remained white after sudden cooling, but became black again after superfusion when brought into contact with white or black phosphorus. Most of the specimen dissolved in carbon disulphide, leaving only a trace of very pale yellow matter that seemed to be amorphous phosphorus.

l: P. THENARD, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, [Illustration] BLACK PHOSPHORUS.
s: P. Thenard challenges the customary explanation of black phosphorus as a mixture of ordinary phosphorus with traces of a metallic phosphide. He submitted a specimen of black or dark gray phosphorus to the Academy and reported its changes under melting, cooling, superfusion, and contact with other forms of phosphorus.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COMPOSITION OF STEEP WATER.
s: The unit describes the composition of water in which malt has been steeped, according to M. C. Leeuw. It contains 0.56 percent organic matter and 0.52 percent mineral matter, for a total of 1.08 percent dry matter, including 0.033 percent nitrogen. Its mineral matter includes potash, phosphoric acid, lime, soda, magnesia, sulphuric acid, traces of oxide of iron, and no chlorine or silica.

l: steep water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COMPOSITION OF STEEP WATER.
s: Steep water is water in which malt has been steeped. According to M. C. Leeuw, it contains 1.08 percent total dry matter, consisting of 0.56 percent organic matter and 0.52 percent mineral matter, and contains 0.033 percent nitrogen.

l: composition of steep water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COMPOSITION OF STEEP WATER.
s: The composition of steep water includes 0.193 percent potash, 0.031 percent phosphoric acid, 0.012 percent lime, 0.047 percent soda, 0.016 percent magnesia, and 0.007 percent sulphuric acid. Oxide of iron is present in traces, while chlorine and silica are absent.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
s: Schreiber's apparatus revivifies bone-black by washing it with water and acid in a rotary washer, then drying, reheating, and cooling it for reuse. The apparatus includes filters, wells, a washer, an elevator, an automatic drying system, and a continuous furnace. The animal black furnace uses undulating cast-iron retorts heated by a coke fire, followed by cooling pipes that deliver the treated black ready for bagging. An apparatus of the described dimensions can revivify 120 hectoliters of bone-black in twenty-four hours using 360 to 400 kilogrammes of coke.

l: Schreiber's apparatus for revivifying bone-black, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
s: Schreiber's apparatus transfers used bone-black from wells to a rotary washer, then uses a steam filter, elevator, drier, furnace retorts, and cooling pipes to process it continuously. Its elevator and gearing operate automatically after the gearing lever is engaged.

l: bone-black, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
s: Bone-black loses its decolorizing properties when its pores become filled with absorbed salts and insoluble compounds from sugar refining. In the apparatus, it is washed, elevated while wet, dried, revivified in heated retorts, cooled, and discharged ready to be bagged and reused.

l: revivification of bone-black, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
s: Revivification frees bone-black from absorbed salts and insoluble compounds so that it can be used again. The text describes fermentation and washing as methods, noting a tendency to abandon fermentation in favor of washing with water and acid in a rotary washer.

l: rotary washer, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
s: The rotary washer receives bone-black directly from the wells and discharges it near a steam filter beneath the floor. The steam filter directs the wet black toward an elevator, which carries it to the drier.

l: automatic drying system, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
s: The automatic drying system is located at the upper part of the furnace and was devised to dry bone-black as it exits the washer. It consists of two undulating pipes with openings for steam to escape, while waste heat and combustion products pass through the space between them before leaving through the chimney.

l: animal black furnace, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
s: The animal black furnace has a masonry casing, a coke-fired chamber, and two rows of undulating cast-iron retorts enclosed in refractory clay blocks. Bone-black passes from the hopper through the drier, retorts, and cooling pipes; the cooling pipes end in rotary cylinders that regulate its discharge into a rail car. The furnace can revivify 120 hectoliters of bone-black in twenty-four hours with 360 to 400 kilogrammes of coke.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: The article explains to consumers how to make pure, neutral potash soap and contrasts it with soda soap.
