It recommends cotton seed oil for manufacturers and laundry soap, warns that products sold as crystal, ball, or rock potash are actually caustic soda, and discusses the possible benefits of fleece scouring for sheep owners.

l: soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: The article presents practical instructions for consumers to make pure and unadulterated soap. It explains that soap made with tallow or grease can be nearly as hard as soda soap, while soap made with oil can be remelted with water to produce a bright, harder, and stiffer product.

l: consumers, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: Consumers are shown how to make neutral potash soap for household and laundry use. The article cautions them to distinguish genuine caustic potash from products falsely sold as potash.

l: potash soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: Potash soap is described as superior to soda soap, especially for washing wool or woolen fabrics. When made with pure caustic potash, it can be neutral and suitable for wool washing, household use, and laundry purposes.

l: soda soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: Soda soap is compared unfavorably with potash soap, particularly for washing wool or woolen fabrics. The article states that potash soap is superior to soda soap even when the soda soap is pure and well made.

l: caustic potassa, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: Pure caustic potash is used to make neutral potash soap. Twenty pounds are dissolved in two gallons of water, cooled to about 90 F, and mixed with eighty pounds of melted tallow, grease, or oil; the article warns that it melts and deteriorates quickly when exposed to air.

l: caustic soda, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: Caustic soda is described as a different substance from caustic potash, although the two look alike. Products called crystal potash, ball potash, or rock potash are said to contain caustic soda, often adulterated, rather than potash.

l: hard soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: The method for making pure neutral potash soap is said to be almost identical to the method for making hard soap with pure powdered caustic soda. Potash soap made with tallow can become nearly as hard as soda soap.

l: wool and woolen fabrics, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: Potash soap is recommended for washing wool and woolen fabrics because it is considered superior to soda soap for this purpose. The article says it can be used to wash wool and the cloth made from it.

l: tallow or grease, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: Tallow or grease should be free from salt before being used to make potash soap. Eighty pounds are melted, cooled to about 130 F, and mixed with caustic potash lye; the article identifies these materials as economical and readily available to farmers and householders.

l: cotton seed oil, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: Cotton seed oil is recommended for manufacturers or for making laundry soap. The article says it produces a magnificent soap that lathers very freely.

l: fleece scouring, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
s: Fleece scouring involves washing wool while it is still growing on the sheep with potash soap made from waste tallow available on sheep farms. The article says it could benefit sheep owners by improving the condition of their wool and cleaning the sheep's skin.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
s: S.S. Bradford reports on using cotton seed oil in place of olive oil for lead plaster and several pharmacopoeial liniments. He found that cotton seed oil produced lead plaster of equally good quality when one and one-half pints of boiling water were used instead of one-half pint. It performed well in Linimentum Ammoniae, Linimentum Camphorae, and Linimentum Chloroformi, but was unsuitable for Linimentum Calcis. Bradford also observed that cotton seed oil turned reddish when mixed with liquor plumbi subacetatis, providing a way to detect small amounts of it in olive oil.

l: S.S. Bradford, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
s: S.S. Bradford had manufactured lead plaster for six years and investigated whether cotton seed oil could replace olive oil. He also tested cotton seed oil in several pharmacopoeial liniments and reported its effects.

l: cotton seed oil, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
s: Cotton seed oil can be used to make lead plaster of equally good quality as plaster made with olive oil when one and one-half pints of boiling water are added. It makes a better-consistency Linimentum Ammoniae, is superior to olive oil for dissolving camphor in Linimentum Camphorae, and performs well in Linimentum Chloroformi, but it is unsuitable for Linimentum Calcis because it does not readily saponify and separates quickly. When mixed with liquor plumbi subacetatis, it turns reddish after twelve to twenty-four hours, a change detectable in mixtures containing five percent or less cotton seed oil.

l: lead plaster, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
s: Lead plaster made with cotton seed oil was found by S.S. Bradford to be equally as good as that made with olive oil when the U. S. P. process was modified by using one and one-half pints of boiling water instead of one-half pint.

l: olive oil, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
s: Olive oil was the oil traditionally used by S.S. Bradford for lead plaster and was compared with cotton seed oil in several liniments. When pure olive oil is mixed with liquor plumbi subacetatis, it does not undergo the reddish color change observed with cotton seed oil.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Prof. de Chaumont’s lecture explains how food is used to build and repair the human body, produce energy, and generate animal heat. It classifies food into nitrogenous substances, fats, starches and sugars, salts, water, and air, emphasizing the need for adequate quantities and variety. The lecture also discusses alcohol, tea, coffee, tobacco, and oatmeal gruel in relation to fatigue and useful work. It concludes by addressing scurvy outbreaks among seamen and urging varied provisions, including potatoes and lime-juice, aboard ships.

l: Prof. de Chaumont, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Prof. de Chaumont delivered a lecture at the Sanitary Congress at Newcastle-on-Tyne on September 28, 1882. He discussed the uses and classes of food, the energy of the body, alcohol, fatigue, tobacco, and scurvy among seamen.

l: man, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Man is described as probably naturally frugivorous, like the monkeys, though he began eating animal food many ages ago. His digestive apparatus appears adapted to food capable of yielding nutriment, and his system can accommodate itself to changes in diet.

l: food, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Food is defined as any substance taken into the body and used to build or repair tissues, provide energy and animal heat, or control or assist those functions. The definition includes water and air, although they are not ordinarily recognized as food.

l: human nutrition, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Human nutrition is best maintained by a due admixture and variety of the four classes of aliment discussed in the lecture. Water and salts are also required, and monotony of diet can seriously affect health, digestion, and assimilation.

l: energy of the body, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: The energy of the body is derived from food, particularly from its non-nitrogenous parts. Heat is described as a form of convertible energy that can perform useful or productive work.

l: organic substances, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Organic substances are divided into nitrogen-containing substances and substances that do not contain nitrogen. The latter include fats, starches, and sugars.

l: nitrogenous substances, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Nitrogenous substances are needed to build up tissues in the young and repair and renew them in adults. They include animal albumin, fibrin, myosin or synronin, casein, blood substances, and vegetable glutin and legumin; they also contribute to bodily energy when broken down and oxidized.

l: non-nitrogenous food, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Non-nitrogenous food includes fats, starches, and sugars. Modern experiments are said to show that these substances, rather than the nitrogenous part of food, provide most of the body's energy.

l: fats, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Fats are non-nitrogenous constituents that contribute energy. Examples recommended in a varied diet include butter, lard, suet, and oil.

l: starches and sugars, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Starches and sugars are non-nitrogenous food constituents that provide energy. Examples include starch from wheat, potatoes, rice, and peas, as well as cane-sugar and milk-sugar.

l: human body, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: The human body is compared to a machine or engine that requires fuel in proportion to the work performed and the speed at which it is done. Its tissues and fluids, except fat, contain nitrogen, and its processes follow universal physical laws.

l: alcohol, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Alcohol may be a comfort and blessing when properly used but becomes a bane and curse in excess. Experiments at Netley indicated that beyond an amount represented by about one and a half to two pints of beer, it provided no convertible energy; it could give a temporary stimulus followed by depression and was generally not given before or during work.

l: scurvy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Scurvy is presented as a serious maritime health problem associated with inadequate or monotonous provisions. Its prevention may require varied food, proper supplies of lime-juice, and substantial provisions of fresh and dried potatoes.

l: scientific experiments on food and energy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Scientific experiments and the work of Joule, Lyon Playfair, Clausius, Tyndall, Helmholtz, and others established that heat is a mode of motion and convertible energy. Experiments by Dr. Parkes at the laboratory at Netley showed that alcohol beyond a limited amount did not provide convertible energy.

l: scurvy outbreaks, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: Scurvy outbreaks had increased again, reaching ninety-nine in 1881, after a serious falling off since 1873. Mr. Thomas Gray attributed this possibly to neglect of varied food scales, and the lecture also suggests neglect of regulations concerning lime-juice.

l: lecture on food and energy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
s: The lecture on food and energy explains the classification and uses of food, the relation between nutrition and bodily work, and the importance of variety in diet. It also considers alcohol and other restoratives, tobacco, scurvy among seamen, and the need for shipowners or the legislature to protect maritime health.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Henry H. Croft discusses whether rattlesnake poison is an alkaloid and reports tests of its reaction with iodine. Mr. Pedler had reported that platinic chloride destroys or neutralizes snake poison, probably by forming an insoluble double platinic chloride. Croft observed a dense light-brown precipitate when iodine solution was added to poison from a rattlesnake, and he describes iodine in potassium iodide as a favored Texas remedy for rattlesnake bites. He questions the usefulness of potassium permanganate after poison has been absorbed and reports finding ammonium urate in the snake's bladder.

l: Henry H. Croft, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Henry H. Croft reports experiments and observations on rattlesnake poison in Texas. He tested poison from a rattlesnake with iodine solution, considered possible chemical explanations for remedies, and questioned the therapeutic value of potassium permanganate after absorption.

l: Mr. Pedler, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Mr. Pedler reported that snake poison is destroyed or neutralized by platinic chloride, probably through formation of an insoluble double platinic chloride. He also referred to potassium permanganate but allowed that it would probably be ineffective after the poison had been absorbed.

l: Texas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Texas is described as a place where rattlesnakes are very common and people camping out are exposed to their bites. Croft conducted his observations there, at Hermanitas Ranch, far from chemical laboratories.

l: rattlesnake poison, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Rattlesnake poison was suggested to be an alkaloid-like substance. Poison taken from a fully charged rattlesnake gland produced a dense light-brown, apparently amorphous precipitate when iodine solution was added.

l: rattlesnake, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Croft killed a moderately sized rattlesnake identified as Crotalus horridus that had not bitten anything. Its poison gland was fully charged with white, opaque poison, and its bladder contained a considerable quantity of light-brown amorphous ammonium urate.

l: rattlesnake bites, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Croft says iodine in potassium iodide is a favored remedy for rattlesnake bites in Texas. He reports having observed the mixture's efficacy in two cases, one involving a buck and the other a dog.

l: iodine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Iodine was proposed as a possible antidotal agent because it formed a precipitate with rattlesnake poison, as it does with many alkaloids. Croft observed a dense light-brown precipitate immediately after adding iodine solution to the poison.

l: potassium iodide, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: A strong solution of iodine in potassium iodide is described as a popular Texas remedy for rattlesnake bites. Potassium iodide can also be combined with ferric chloride to make an extemporaneous solution for testing alkaloids and perhaps snake poison.

l: iodine solution, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Iodine solution was applied in reported cases of rattlesnake bites and was tested directly on rattlesnake poison. It immediately produced a dense light-brown precipitate with no crystalline structure visible under the microscope.

l: platinic chloride, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: Platinic chloride was reported by Mr. Pedler to destroy or neutralize snake poison. Croft attributes this action probably to formation of an insoluble double platinic chloride, as occurs with almost all alkaloids.

l: alkaloids, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
s: The poisonous principle in snakes was described by a French chemist as possibly belonging to the alkaloids. Croft compared the reaction of rattlesnake poison with iodine to the precipitates produced by most alkaloids and mentions a ferric chloride and potassium iodide mixture as a convenient alkaloid test.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: The unit describes the use of finger and palm impressions as signatures in China, especially in courts, the army, and certain domestic transactions. Chinese courts require criminals to validate confessions with a thumb-print, while digital signatures are also used to prevent personation and repudiation. The text discusses observations by Henry Faulds and W. J. Herschel concerning skin-furrows, heredity, government registration, medical jurisprudence, and ethnology. It concludes that Chinese and European finger rugae differ, but their variation is too great for reliable ethnic or hereditary classification.

l: The Chinese Sign Manual, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: The Chinese Sign Manual concerns the use of finger, thumb, and palm impressions as signatures in China. It describes their application in courts, the army, and transactions involving the sale or divorce of persons.

l: Henry Faulds, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Henry Faulds solicits information from China about skin-furrows on the hand. His observations on Japanese finger-tips are described as having an ethnic bearing and relating to heredity.

l: W. J. Herschel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: W. J. Herschel solicits information about skin-furrows on the hand. After twenty years in charge of registration offices in India, he employed finger marks as sign manuals to prevent personation and repudiation.

l: China, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: China uses digital impressions as sign manuals in courts, the army, and certain domestic transactions. The text states that the practice may have become common after the Han period.

l: India, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: India is where W. J. Herschel employed finger marks in registration offices for twenty years to prevent personation and repudiation.

l: skin-furrows on the hand, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Skin-furrows on the hand are the subject on which Henry Faulds and W. J. Herschel solicit information. The unit treats them as relevant to sign manuals, medical jurisprudence, and ethnology.

l: medical jurisprudence, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Medical jurisprudence is identified as one field to which the study of skin-furrows may have a bearing. The unit particularly connects digital signatures with the legal validation of confessions.

l: ethnology, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Ethnology is identified as another field potentially affected by the study of skin-furrows. The text concludes that finger rugae do not provide a reliable basis for distinguishing populations.

l: heredity, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Heredity is connected with Henry Faulds's observations on the finger-tips of the Japanese. The unit concludes that finger striae are not a basis for studying heredity.

l: fingerprint identification, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Fingerprint identification is represented by the use of finger, thumb, and palm impressions as sign manuals. The text considers such marks difficult to forge or repudiate because the finger rugae remain substantially unchanged from the cradle to the grave.

l: Chinese courts, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Chinese courts require criminals to sign confessions by impressing the whorls of their thumb-tips. Women use the right thumb and men the left, and a confession is not legally valid without the prisoner's thumb-print.

l: the army, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: The army sometimes requires digital signatures to prevent personation. The general in command at Wenchow enforces the practice among his troops, and descriptions of persons note the relative numbers of volutes and coniferous finger-tips.

l: criminals, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Criminals in Chinese courts must attest their confessions with thumb-prints before they can legally be executed. A contumacious culprit may be tortured until he performs this required act.

l: confession, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: A confession is required for the legal execution of a criminal in the Chinese courts. It must be attested by the prisoner's thumb-print to be valid.

l: personation and repudiation, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Personation and repudiation are the acts that finger marks are used to prevent in Indian registration offices and in military applications. The text also describes digital signatures as difficult to forge or repudiate.

l: Chinese people, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: The Chinese people's finger rugae are said to differ from those of Europeans. However, the text finds too little uniformity among them for the rugae to serve as a basis for ethnic distinction or heredity.

l: Europeans, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
s: Europeans are used as a comparison group for Chinese finger rugae. The text states that Chinese and European rugae differ, but that the observed variation does not support reliable ethnic classification.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: Matthew Arnold argued that lucidity was the great need of England and an indispensable condition for serious intellectual and spiritual construction. He contrasted the French national tendency toward lucidity with the English national tendency toward seriousness, while warning that both qualities could be accompanied by serious defects. He identified Voltaire as the chief agent of France's eighteenth-century movement toward lucidity and compared him with Luther. Arnold criticized the Salvation Army and the Oxford movement associated with Dr. Pusey for building on assumptions that lucidity would have exposed as no longer valid, and he endorsed schools and universities as the best means of cultivating lucidity.

l: Matthew Arnold, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: Matthew Arnold said that the word he wished to leave in his audience's memories was lucidity. He identified lucidity as England's great want and argued that schools and universities could help cultivate it.

l: lucidity, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: Lucidity is the perception that notions long current lack truth and validity, are no longer possible, and can no longer serve. Arnold presents it as inevitable and indispensable, and as the condition of all serious construction for the future.

l: France, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: France is described as having a national turn for lucidity. Its eighteenth-century movement toward lucidity was associated particularly with Voltaire, although France's lucidity was accompanied by faults such as a want of seriousness and reverence.

l: England, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: England is described as having a national turn for seriousness rather than lucidity. Its thinkers often drew back from free inquiry when it conflicted with established beliefs and conventions, and Arnold said that England had not yet founded the reign of lucidity.

l: French people, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: The French people are described as having a national turn for lucidity. They are also said to display, alongside lucidity, a want of seriousness and reverence.

l: English people, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: The English people are described as naturally serious and as possessing reverence, respect, and love for the past. Arnold suggested that lucidity, when it came among them, might be joined to these qualities without the dangers seen elsewhere.

l: seriousness, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: Seriousness is presented as a valuable and indispensable quality of England, even though it may be accompanied by false ideas, prejudice, and other disagreeable defects. Arnold contrasts it with the French tendency toward lucidity.

l: Voltaire, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: Voltaire is identified as the principal agent of France's eighteenth-century travail for lucidity. Although Arnold says that Voltaire harmed France through his lack of seriousness and reverence, he credits Voltaire's lucidity with doing good and compares him to the Luther of the eighteenth-century cultivated classes.

l: Luther, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: Luther is admired for working for conduct, which Arnold says was more than working merely for intelligence. Like Voltaire, Luther opposed the object of his antipathy with conviction, energy, genius, and masterly power, carrying his world with him.

l: Salvation Army, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: The Salvation Army is presented as a movement displaying numbers, funds, energy, devotedness, excitement, and conversions, but a total absence of lucidity. Arnold says that a little lucidity would make the movement impossible because it assumes a basis that is no longer possible or receivable.

l: Dr. Pusey, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: Dr. Pusey is described as having recently ended a long, devoted, laborious, influential, pure, and pathetic life. The movement associated with his earlier name is said to have produced people worthy of respect, admiration, and love, but also to have rested on assumptions that lucidity would have exposed as unsound.

l: schools and universities, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
s: Schools and universities are presented as the best agency for generating lucidity, especially through serious and disinterested studies connected with one another and continued into adult life. Arnold says that this process may be slow but is sure.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: The unit describes apparatus and experiments designed to protect people entering flames, focusing on Humphry Davy's wire-gauze discovery and Chevalier Aldini's protective suit. Aldini's demonstrations included handling hot iron, walking over fires, breathing amid flames, and entering burning passages while shielded by metallic gauze and asbestos cloth. Hot-house and furnace experiments involving Joseph Banks, Charles Blagden, Dr. Solander, and others showed that people could withstand very high dry temperatures, partly because perspiration cools the body. The account also considers human respiration in flames and proposes that Egyptian mystery fire-walking may have used a concealed fire beneath a grate.

l: apparatus for entering flames, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: The apparatus was designed to let a person enter flames without being burned. It consisted mainly of metallic-gauze armor, including a helmet, cuirass, skirt, boots, and a shield, combined with coarse alum-soaked clothing and asbestos coverings for the head, hands, and feet.

l: Humphry Davy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: Humphry Davy observed that very fine wire gauze cooled a flame so that it could not pass through the meshes. He attributed the effect to the metal's conductivity and radiating power and used it in constructing a miners' lamp.

l: Chevalier Aldini, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: Chevalier Aldini applied Davy's wire-gauze discovery to an envelope intended to allow a person to enter flames. He traveled through Europe giving free demonstrations of the apparatus, including demonstrations before a committee of the Academic des Sciences in Paris.

l: metallic gauze, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: Metallic gauze cooled flames enough to prevent them from traversing its meshes. In Aldini's apparatus it formed the protective armor, double-gauze boots, and a shield, and it was also used to cover a basket carrying a child.

l: asbestos cloth, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: Asbestos cloth covered the wearer's head, hands, and feet beneath or within the metallic-gauze apparatus. A single layer was used for the bonnet and stockings, while double layers formed the gloves, and a child carried into flames wore an asbestos bonnet.

l: Aldini's demonstrations, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: Aldini's demonstrations began with holding a finger wrapped in asbestos and double wire gauze in a candle or alcohol flame. Assistants also handled red-hot iron, carried firebrands over burning fagots, and entered intense flames while wearing the protective apparatus.

l: Paris, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: In Paris, an exhibition was held before a committee from the Academic des Sciences. Two burning straw fences formed a passage through which six men wearing Aldini suits walked, while one carried an eight-year-old child in a wire-gauze-covered basket.

l: Aldini's six experimenters, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: Six men wearing Aldini suits entered the passage between two blazing straw fences and walked slowly backward and forward while the fire was fed from outside. One of them carried an eight-year-old child who wore only an asbestos bonnet.

l: fire-walking demonstrations, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: In some demonstrations, experimenters holding firebrands walked for five minutes over a large grating beneath which fagots were burning. Aldini's six experimenters also walked through a narrow passage between blazing fences, and one man later entered a clear fire whose flames rose eighteen feet while carrying a child.

l: hot-house experiments, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: Joseph Banks, Charles Blagden, and Dr. Solander remained for ten minutes in a hot-house at 211 degrees Fahrenheit while their bodies stayed near normal temperature. Blagden later endured eight minutes in a hot-house reaching 262 degrees Fahrenheit, while eggs placed nearby were baked hard in twenty minutes.

l: human resistance to heat, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: The unit attributes human resistance to high temperatures partly to reduced carbonic-acid exhalation and reduced internal combustion as external heat rises. It also emphasizes that dry, moving air is more tolerable than humid air because evaporation of perspiration cools the body, while contact with hot liquids or solids is especially dangerous.

l: human respiration in flames, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: The experiments are presented as evidence that a person can breathe in the midst of flames. This ability is attributed not only to cooling as air passes through wire gauze but also to the human organs' considerable resistance to heat.

l: Egyptian mysteries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
s: The unit considers whether initiation rites connected with the Egyptian mysteries may have involved crossing a burning chamber over an incandescent grate. It suggests that the account in the Abbe Terrason's "Sethos" may be better explained by a fire in a ditch beneath a grate, which would prevent flames from reaching the person crossing it.

l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: The unit describes the development and distribution of the building stone supply in the United States, including granite, sandstone or freestone, limestone, marble, slate, and other stones. It explains that early settlers mainly used wood and imported brick and stone, but American quarrying expanded during the nineteenth century. Major quarrying centers and uses are identified, including construction, paving, monuments, lime production, roofing, and sidewalks. The account names notable buildings, quarries, and regions associated with these materials.

l: building stone supply, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: The building stone supply developed slowly in the United States because early settlers relied mainly on wood and imported brick and stone. The unit traces the growth of domestic quarrying and describes the principal American sources and uses of granite, freestone, limestone, marble, slate, and other stones.

l: stone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: Stone was used only slightly as a building material in the early history of the country. Loose stone was readily gathered for foundations, while more substantial building stone was initially imported by Dutch and English settlers.

l: Boston, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: Boston used imported brick, tile, slate, and stone in its early buildings. King's Chapel in Boston was identified as the first recorded building constructed from American stone.

l: King's Chapel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: King's Chapel in Boston was erected in 1752 and is recorded as the first building made from American stone. Its stone was granite brought from Braintree, Massachusetts.

l: granite, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: Granite is particularly abundant in New England and occurs in lesser quantities elsewhere in the country. It was used for major buildings, monuments, paving, and breakwaters, and could be quarried into blocks of almost any size and shape.

l: New England, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: New England contains especially abundant granite and also has sandstone, marble, and slate sources. Granite from the region became an important building material, while much of its marble was described as inferior to that of Vermont and Berkshire, Massachusetts.

l: Quincy granite, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: Quincy granite was used in the old Merchants' Exchange and Astor House in New York, the Custom House in New Orleans, and many other buildings along the Atlantic coast. It weighs about 165 pounds per cubic foot and was shipped to distant markets.

l: Quincy quarries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: The Quincy quarries were the first granite quarries in the country to be extensively developed, with work beginning early in the nineteenth century. The first railroad in the country, a three-mile horse railroad built in 1827, was constructed from these quarries to the Neponset River.

l: Quincy, Mass., Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: Quincy, Massachusetts, became an important center of granite production early in the nineteenth century. Its granite was transported to distant markets, including New Orleans, and was used in numerous prominent buildings.

l: New York, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: New York used Quincy granite in the old Merchants' Exchange and Astor House, and its old City Hall and Custom House were among the early marble buildings. New York also obtained granite from Staten Island and sandstone from Portland and other quarrying regions.

l: freestone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: Freestone, or sandstone, came into use earlier than granite, although its American use was still relatively late. It was used for buildings, paving, curbing, sidewalks, and furnace hearth-stones.

l: Portland quarries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: The Portland quarries, opposite Middletown on the Connecticut River, were worked before the Revolution and shipped sandstone to many distant parts of the country. Their stone was also associated with the fossil bird footprints discovered there in 1802.

l: Portland stone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: Portland stone supplied most of the brownstone fronts in New York City, although some buildings used thin layers of it over brick walls. It was widely distributed from the Portland quarries.

l: limestone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
s: Limestone was used for building where granite or sandstone was not readily available, and hammer-dressed limestone could resemble granite. It was also widely used for roads and sidewalks and was burned into lime, although the quality of lime varied by region.
